2026 Pokémon Mega Evolution —Delta Reign Preview: Top Cards And Investing Outlook

  • By Jesse Haynes
  • on September 8th, 2026
  • in Releases
Contents show topics
1 Why Delta Reign matters
2 Mega Rayquaza ex Special Illustration Rare
3 Mega Rayquaza ex Mega Ultra Rare
4 Raikou ex Special Illustration Rare
5 Zinnia’s Trust Special Illustration Rare
6 Groudon Illustration Rare
7 Is Delta Reign a Good Pokémon set to invest in?
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 8:26
Instaread

The Pokémon TCG’s Mega Evolution era is about to get one of its biggest names yet.

Pokémon Mega Evolution—Delta Reign arrives November 6, 2026, with Mega Rayquaza ex serving as the centerpiece of a set that could become one of the more interesting releases of the current Mega Evolution cycle.

Pokémon has confirmed that Delta Reign will contain more than 135 cards, including four new Mega Evolution Pokémon ex: Mega Rayquaza ex, Mega Golurk ex, Mega Malamar ex and Mega Golisopod ex, along with more than 35 cards featuring special illustrations.

The set will also include 14 Illustration Rare Pokémon, 17 Ultra Rare Pokémon and Trainer cards, and six Special Illustration Rare cards.

Most importantly for collectors, however, we already have an unusually good idea of what Delta Reign will look like.

The bulk of the expansion originates from the Japanese Storm Emeralda set, which released July 31. Delta Reign is expected to combine Storm Emeralda with cards from three Japanese Mega starter decks, making it slightly larger than many of the recent English Mega Evolution expansions.

And that gives us an early look at the cards collectors are likely to chase.

Why Delta Reign matters

There are two reasons Delta Reign should have considerably more collector interest than something like Pitch Black.

The first is obvious: Rayquaza.

Rayquaza has been one of the hobby’s premier Pokémon for years, with many older Rayquaza cards developing substantial collector followings. Even before Delta Reign’s release, collectors were speculating that the return of Mega Rayquaza could provide a boost to older Rayquaza cards.

In a July discussion on r/PokeInvesting, the general consensus was that Delta Reign would easily outdraw several of the preceding Mega Evolution sets, although some collectors cautioned that it could ultimately become a “one card carries the set” release.

That last part may prove important.

The Japanese market for Storm Emeralda has already established a remarkably clear hierarchy. Mega Rayquaza dominates the set, while prices fall off dramatically after the top two cards.

The second reason Delta Reign is interesting is its new Legendary Stadium mechanic. The Stadiums are split across two cards that connect visually, somewhat reminiscent of the LEGEND cards from the HeartGold & SoulSilver era. It gives Delta Reign a little extra identity beyond simply being “the Rayquaza set.”

Still, neither feature necessarily makes Delta Reign a must-buy investment.

Its November 6 release also places it alongside major Pokémon 30th-anniversary product, which could soak up a tremendous amount of collector spending. That concern is already showing up in investing communities, where some collectors believe the 30th Anniversary releases will overshadow Delta Reign in the short term.

For buyers willing to be patient, that may actually create opportunity.

Mega Rayquaza ex Special Illustration Rare

There is no question about the biggest traditional chase card in Delta Reign.

The Mega Rayquaza ex Special Illustration Rare features artwork from Kazuki Minami, winner of the 2024 Pokémon TCG Illustration Contest. It is only the second Pokémon TCG card illustrated by Minami.

More importantly, Japanese collectors have already voted with their wallets.

Shortly after Storm Emeralda released, the Mega Rayquaza SIR was valued at roughly 82,800 yen, or around $550 at the time. Several weeks later, Japanese market tracking still had the card around the $400-$500 range.

That is an enormous gap between Rayquaza and nearly everything else in the set.

For collectors, this is the card I would watch most closely after release. But I would also be extremely hesitant to buy during the opening-week frenzy. Modern Pokémon chase cards routinely begin with enormous premiums before supply catches up.

Investment outlook: Excellent card, questionable release-week purchase.

Mega Rayquaza ex Mega Ultra Rare

Technically, the rarest and most expensive card from Storm Emeralda has actually been the gold Mega Rayquaza ex Mega Ultra Rare.

Early Japanese prices exceeded $1,000, with the card commanding an enormous premium because of the difficulty of pulling the Mega Ultra Rare rarity.

I expect the English version to become one of Delta Reign’s marquee trophies as well.

The caveat is aesthetics. Ultra-low print rates can create enormous values, but collector demand matters just as much over the long term. For many collectors, the Special Illustration Rare is simply the more visually compelling Rayquaza.

If you’re collecting rather than speculating purely on rarity, I prefer the SIR.

Raikou ex Special Illustration Rare

If there is a clear No. 2 Pokémon chase behind Rayquaza, Raikou ex appears to have claimed the spot.

The Japanese Raikou SIR has consistently been one of Storm Emeralda’s highest-priced non-Rayquaza cards, trading well ahead of the remaining SIRs.

Raikou also has something I like from an investing perspective: established popularity without necessarily receiving the same immediate hype premium attached to Rayquaza.

This is exactly the type of card I would consider buying as a single after the initial post-release decline.

Zinnia’s Trust Special Illustration Rare

Trainer cards have become a somewhat less predictable investment category, but Zinnia’s Trust deserves attention because of its direct connection to Rayquaza lore.

Interestingly, the Japanese version hasn’t been nearly as expensive as some collectors initially expected. Early reporting from PokéBeach specifically noted that Zinnia was lagging behind expectations, while Rayquaza absorbed most of the set’s high-end demand.

That could make it one of Delta Reign’s more interesting sleeper cards if the artwork resonates with English collectors.

I wouldn’t treat it as a centerpiece investment, but it’s one I’d watch.

Groudon Illustration Rare

Not every worthwhile card has to cost hundreds of dollars.

The Groudon Illustration Rare is exactly the type of card I increasingly like targeting from modern Pokémon sets: recognizable Pokémon, strong artwork and a much lower entry point than the headline chase.

Japanese pricing has placed Groudon among the more desirable Illustration Rares in Storm Emeralda, alongside cards such as Kecleon and Growlithe.

These lower-tier Illustration Rares may ultimately provide better value for collectors than paying hundreds of dollars for Rayquaza immediately after release.

One notable omission is Kyogre. Although its Illustration Rare appears in Storm Emeralda, PokéBeach reports that Pokémon is removing it from the regular English checklist and using the artwork as the Delta Reign Elite Trainer Box promo instead.

That makes the ETB itself considerably more appealing.

Is Delta Reign a Good Pokémon set to invest in?

This is where I think the comparisons to Pitch Black make some sense—but only to a point.

Pitch Black developed plenty of defenders because of its artwork, but from an investing perspective it has lacked the depth of marquee chase Pokémon that typically drives elite sets.

Even recent Reddit discussions asking why Pitch Black was considered weak repeatedly pointed toward the limited speculative demand surrounding the release.

Delta Reign has a trump card Pitch Black doesn’t have: Mega Rayquaza.

But I don’t think that automatically makes Delta Reign a top-tier investment set.

Right now, it looks somewhat top-heavy. Rayquaza is spectacular. Raikou is strong. Zinnia has appeal. There are several excellent Illustration Rares. But there is a big difference between that and a truly deep release with five, six or seven cards collectors desperately want.

That leads to a fairly simple strategy.

Don’t chase Delta Reign at peak hype.

If booster boxes and ETBs immediately soar above MSRP, I would be patient. Pokémon’s 30th Anniversary is going to compete heavily for collector dollars, and Reddit investors are already speculating that Delta Reign could be easier to obtain because of it.

For sealed collectors, that could create a much better buying window after launch.

For singles collectors, I particularly like waiting for the first major supply wave and targeting Mega Rayquaza SIR, Raikou SIR and some of the stronger Illustration Rares once prices settle.

Delta Reign probably isn’t the best Pokémon set of 2026.

But with Mega Rayquaza at the center of it, it’s also going to be very difficult for collectors to ignore.

And if the 30th Anniversary temporarily steals the spotlight in November, being overlooked at release might actually be the best thing that could happen to Delta Reign as a long-term collectible.
